name: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
title: Threat Modelling for Legal AI
answer: Threat modelling for legal AI identifies ways a legal AI system can fail, be misused, or be attacked, and maps those failures to harm for clients, lawyers, and courts. It covers confidentiality of case data, integrity of legal reasoning, availability of tools during deadlines, and accountability for outputs. The scope includes both internal tools used by law firms and client-facing systems that draft, review, or predict legal outcomes. It also considers supply chain risks from third-party models and data providers.

sections.body: Threat modelling for legal AI identifies ways a legal AI system can fail, be misused, or be attacked, and maps those failures to harm for clients, lawyers, and courts. It covers confidentiality of case data, integrity of legal reasoning, availability of tools during deadlines, and accountability for outputs. The scope includes both internal tools used by law firms and client-facing systems that draft, review, or predict legal outcomes. It also considers supply chain risks from third-party models and data providers.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Legal AI threat modelling runs on the same infrastructure as the systems it audits: cloud or on-premises model hosting, document repositories, retrieval pipelines, and user access layers. It requires an asset inventory of models, prompts, embeddings, and case data, plus logs of queries and outputs. The work often uses threat libraries adapted from software security, such as STRIDE or attack trees, but applied to model behaviour and legal workflows. No special hardware is needed beyond standard security tooling and access to the system under review.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by assembling a cross-functional group of lawyers, security staff, and AI engineers who walk through realistic misuse scenarios. They ask what an adversary, a careless user, or a faulty model could do at each stage: data ingestion, retrieval, generation, and human review. For each threat they rate likelihood and impact, then choose controls such as access limits, output verification, or prompt filtering. The output is a living threat register that is updated when the model, data, or legal use case changes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in legal AI threat modelling centre on client confidentiality, privilege, and the duty of competence. A model that leaks one client's matter into another's output, or that invents a case citation, creates professional and legal exposure. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which show how courts are beginning to assign responsibility for AI failures. Provenance matters: a threat model should record which model version, training data, and prompts produced a given output so that harm can be traced and remedied. This is not legal advice, but a description of how practitioners approach these duties.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Threat modelling for legal AI is moving from one-off security reviews to continuous, evidence-based assurance. As courts issue more rulings on AI liability and state legislatures pass new AI bills, the threat register will need to absorb new legal duties and technical attack patterns. Expect closer coupling between model evaluation, red teaming, and legal compliance workflows, with threat models feeding directly into client-facing disclosures and audit reports. The goal is not to eliminate risk but to make it visible and manageable before a matter is harmed.
